performers: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; Fritz Reiner, conductor
intro: The horns give a summons, and the strings answer with strummed chords and a headlong Presto. Bartók’s finale sends the whole orchestra chasing its tunes towards F major.

sections.label: Intro · The horns sound a summons
sections.mNote: Pesante: a short horn call and a long pause

sections.label: A · Racing violins, strummed lower strings
sections.mNote: Violas and cellos strum chords beneath racing second violins

sections.label: B · Bassoon dance, then brass
sections.mNote: A bassoon steps forward; brass later sings above running strings

sections.label: Dev · Harps and divided violins
sections.mNote: Quiet string entries overlap beneath short woodwind phrases

sections.label: C · Horns over racing violins
sections.mNote: Horns and brass strengthen the repeated lower-string notes

sections.label: Link · Muted strings and wind replies
sections.mNote: Tranquillo: quiet violins sing beneath slow wind phrases

sections.label: Coda · Strings run beneath long wind lines
sections.mNote: Woodwinds and brass sustain their phrases above the flowing strings

sections.label: Coda · The longer ending
sections.mNote: An acceleration, brass slides and the last rush to F major

cues.title: Horns, then string guitars
cues.text: The horns call out, marked Pesante — heavily. After a long pause, violas and cellos put their bows aside and strum chords like guitars. The second violins start the Presto, playing at the tips of their bows.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, plate B. & H. 9009, p. 79, bars 1–14: Pesante, lunga, quasi chitarra and punta d’arco; Presto at bar 8: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trouble with the finale
cues.text: On 26 September 1943 Bartók writes to his son Péter: “The first 4 are already finished. Now I am having trouble with the last, which for certain reasons is the most difficult.” He is working on the concerto for most of each day.
cues.evidence: Bartók to Péter Bartók, 26 September 1943, quoted by Brett Van Gansbeke from David Cooper, Bartók: Concerto for Orchestra (1996), p. 22: https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto

cues.title: The bassoon steps forward
cues.text: The rushing figures drop away, leaving a bassoon with a sharply pointed tune. Bartók marks it ben marcato. A second bassoon joins, then clarinets, while muted strings tick away underneath.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 97–98, bassoon theme from bar 148, ben marcato; second bassoon entry at bar 152, clarinets at bar 155: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The best orchestra piece
cues.text: Koussevitzky conducts the première with the Boston Symphony on 1 December 1944. Bartók tells a pupil that Koussevitzky calls it “the best orchestra piece of the last 25 years”, the works of his idol Shostakovich included.
cues.evidence: Bartók to a pupil, quoted from Benjamin Suchoff, Bartók: Concerto for Orchestra (1995), p. 115, at https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto. Première date: Richard Rodda, Pittsburgh Symphony programme note, https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf

cues.title: Harps and quiet violins
cues.text: The pace eases to Un poco meno mosso. Two harps strike chords above divided violins; short wind phrases begin darting between the string lines. Some violinists bow the tune while their neighbours pluck the accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 110–111, bars 256–299: two harps, divided violins, woodwind figures and alternating bowed and pizzicato violin parts: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bartók’s pencil in Reiner’s score
cues.text: Reiner conducts from a score corrected by Bartók himself. Paper strips carrying revised passages are pasted over the old ones, and the new ending is inserted after the last page. The score survives at Northwestern University.
cues.evidence: Klára Móricz, Comments, sources CR and RecR: Reiner’s corrected score, paper strips and alternative ending, now in the Fritz Reiner Score Collection at Northwestern University: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf

cues.title: Horns above the running strings
cues.text: The horns stretch a phrase across the violins’ quick notes. Cellos and double basses repeat a short figure below. Trumpets and trombones join with accented replies; then the fast line races through the strings again.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 122–123, bars 394–413: horns, repeated lower-string figures, brass chords and renewed string entries: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violins put on mutes
cues.text: Tranquillo. The first violins sing softly, while the other strings play muted chords. Flutes, oboes, clarinets and horns answer in longer notes. Bartók keeps asking for greater calm.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 128, bars 449–475: Tranquillo, muted string parts, dolce violin melody and sempre più tranquillo: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Long notes over running strings
cues.text: The strings keep their flowing scales while winds and brass lay longer phrases above them. Muted trombone and tuba add a dark line; later the horns and trumpets broaden the sound. The double basses hold notes beneath the rushing bows.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 130–136, bars 498–543: running strings, sustained basses and successive wind and brass lines: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two endings
cues.text: Koussevitzky’s radio broadcast of 30 December 1944 uses Bartók’s original ending. Reiner’s Pittsburgh recording, made in February 1946, uses the longer alternative ending that Bartók supplied.
cues.evidence: Klára Móricz, Comments to the Henle edition, sources A, A-end, RecK (30 December 1944, original ending) and RecR (4–5 February 1946, new ending): https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf

cues.title: The ending Bartók added
cues.text: Reiner plays Bartók’s expanded ending. A fresh acceleration sends the tune between strings and winds; horns and trombones sweep upwards in glissandos. Side drum and cymbal reinforce the final rush into F major.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 145–147, alternative ending, bars 602–625: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Móricz identifies this version in Reiner’s recording, source RecR: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Bows aside, then Presto
transitions.from: Intro · The horns sound a summons
transitions.to: A · Racing violins, strummed lower strings
transitions.how: The horn call ends on a long pause. Violas and cellos put their bows aside, then strum repeated chords, marked quasi chitarra. An acceleration leads to Presto: the second violins run above those chords, with muted horns, timpani and plucked bass notes underneath.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 79, bars 1–14: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: A bassoon emerges from the rush
transitions.from: A · Racing violins, strummed lower strings
transitions.how: The woodwinds stop their running figures one group at a time. Violins, violas and cellos carry on briefly, then dwindle to piano. A bassoon enters with a pointed tune marked ben marcato; another bassoon joins above it. Muted strings beat out short notes beneath them.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 97–98, the approach to bar 148, bassoon entries and muted strings: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: Harps introduce the quiet string entries
transitions.how: Un poco meno mosso begins with quiet harp chords and a held second-violin note. First violins join in divided parts. The low strings rest; plucked notes within the violin sections supply the accompaniment as short flute, clarinet and bassoon phrases appear above.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 110–111, bars 256–299: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: The horns stretch above the violins
transitions.how: The first violins keep running while unmuted horns begin a longer phrase. Cellos and double basses repeat a three-note figure below. Wind chords and brass accents join the crescendo; after a sharp chord, the quick figure starts again in bassoons and low strings.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 122–123, bars 394–413: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: Muted strings soften the violin tune
transitions.to: Link · Muted strings and wind replies
transitions.how: The pace relaxes to Tranquillo. First violins sing piano, dolce, accompanied by muted second violins and violas, with quiet cellos and basses below. Woodwinds answer in long phrases. Horns sustain across the change and later put on mutes.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 128, bars 449–475: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: Low brass beneath the string scales
transitions.from: Link · Muted strings and wind replies
transitions.to: Coda · Strings run beneath long wind lines
transitions.how: Violin, viola and cello scales continue over held double-bass notes. Clarinets sustain above them while muted trombone and tuba enter quietly. The tune passes through cor anglais and other winds; horns and unmuted trumpets join as the strings climb.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 130–136, bars 498–543: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: A longer road to F major
transitions.from: Coda · Strings run beneath long wind lines
transitions.how: The revised ending adds another acceleration. Short wind and string phrases pass over horn and trumpet notes; the double basses rest until the last page. They rejoin the final upward rush, with glissandos from horns and trombones and a side-drum roll. The orchestra lands on F major.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 145–147, bars 602–625: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Móricz, sources A-endR and RecR, identifies the expanded ending used by Reiner: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf

source.title: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra, B. & H. 9009, V, including alternative ending
source.locator: Boosey & Hawkes full score, printed pp. 79–147. The alternative ending on pp. 145–147 is the version identified for Reiner’s 1946 recording in Móricz’s critical-edition commentary.

timeline.note: The horns sound the opening Pesante call (p. 79).
Second violins begin the Presto over strummed viola and cello chords; first violins join the running notes (pp. 79–80).
Winds and brass join the racing strings (pp. 81–90).
A bassoon plays a pointed tune after the string rush subsides (p. 97 onward).
Horns and trumpets sing above running violins and violas (pp. 103–109).
Two harps and divided violins begin the quiet Un poco meno mosso (p. 110).
String entries overlap, with short woodwind phrases darting between them (pp. 111–113).
Long horn phrases and brass accents rise over quick violin notes and repeated lower strings (pp. 122–127).
The Tranquillo begins with a quiet violin tune; woodwinds answer above muted strings (pp. 128–136).
Winds and brass build long phrases over the string scales (pp. 135–144).
The revised ending adds another acceleration, brass glissandos, side drum and cymbal (pp. 145–147).

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending.
fields.note: Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The critical edition identifies this range for the complete recording. The Sony discographical transcription gives 5 February for CD 5 tracks 1–5; individual movement/session allocation is not established. Neither the 1948 issue nor 2010 upload is a session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue stated in the reproduced Columbia session discography. No microphone position or engineer is established for the selected transfer.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: This identifies the original commercial recording, not the unidentified physical or digital carrier from which the Archive MP3 was copied.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The discographical transcription dates MM-793 to 22 November 1948 and ML 4102 to 7 February 1949. Douglas Watt’s March 1949 review independently identifies Columbia set 793 and ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance. The exact carrier used by public-domain-archive.com remains unknown; no sleeve or label scans accompany the selected Archive item.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Complete set: XCO 35800–35811, take 1; LP matrices xLP 539 (I–II), xLP 540 (III–V)
fields.note: These are complete-recording identifiers transcribed from Sony’s discography, not an asserted side-by-side mapping for this MP3. Individual movement matrix boundaries, transfer-side joins and the transferred pressing are unknown. DAHR’s opened Reiner listing does not include these Columbia masters; no DAHR matrix record is fabricated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Archive says only that the files were taken from public-domain-archive.com. Neither transfer engineer nor restoration producer is named. The uploader is not treated as the transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive public date, 8 August 2010, and file modification dates describe repository activity, not the date of analogue transfer or mastering.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original digitisation, equalisation, noise reduction, editing, speed correction and the source carrier are unestablished. The item calls the selected file an original VBR MP3 and supplies Ogg derivatives; this does not identify how the historical master was transferred.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in the EU under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; not a worldwide clearance.
fields.note: Bartók died in 1945; IMSLP identifies this score as public domain in life-plus-70 countries and explicitly warns of continuing US protection. The critical-edition commentary is cited as scholarship, not redistributed as a public-domain score.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963.
fields.note: Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: He heard a future for concert music in village songs, and went out with a phonograph to learn how they were sung.
facts: István Thomán, a Liszt pupil, and Hans Koessler; Budapest Academy, 1899–1903
Piano professor in Budapest, 1907–34; folk-music research in Budapest and at Columbia University
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages; Biskra, 1913; Turkey with Adnan Saygun, 1936
Six quartets, three piano concertos, two violin concertos, three stage works and Mikrokosmos
composer.background:
In May 1904 Bartók went to stay with the Fischer family at Gerlicepuszta. He had a piano sent out, practised four hours a day and composed for four or five more. There he heard Lidi Dósa, a young woman from Transylvania in the family’s service, singing to the children in her care, and began writing down her songs. Here was Hungarian music unlike the urban entertainment that usually went by that name, and he wanted more of it. Two years later, collecting with Bartók, the writer Béla Balázs found that the frail-looking pianist could wear him out: “I was already very tired, but he kept urging and driving me on to collect more!” Balázs put the encounter in his diary.

Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós in 1881, when the town belonged to Hungary; it is now Sânnicolau Mare in Romania. His father, director of an agricultural school, died when he was seven. His mother Paula supported Béla and his sister by teaching, moving between towns before settling in Pozsony, now Bratislava. At the Budapest Academy he studied piano with István Thomán, who had studied with Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler.
